This is LeetCode's Decode String. The pattern is two stacks holding the work a nested group leaves unfinished: one for the repeat count waiting on its
, one for the text built up before that group opened. The words that point to it are "sit inside other groups", nesting that closes most recently opened first, the same shape as matching brackets.

Every character of the decoded result is appended exactly once for each repeat it takes part in, so the cost is O(length of the result), which is what the statement's bound on that length is for. The edge cases are an empty input, a group with no nesting, and two groups back to back rather than nested, which
tests. A single stack of small structs, each holding one group's count and text so far, does the same work and is an equally fair way to write it.

This is LeetCode's K Closest Points to Origin, restated over obstacles. The pattern is a bounded heap that always holds the k obstacles seen so far that are nearest the robot, and drops the farthest of them the moment a nearer one arrives once it is full. The words that point to it are "k obstacles nearest" out of n, with n free to run far larger than k, which is what makes sorting every obstacle the wasteful answer.
Each of the n pushes costs O(log k) against a heap that never grows past size k, so the whole pass is O(n log k) time and O(k) space. The distance is kept as the squared length,
, so no square root and no floating point rounding decides an order the integers already settle exactly.

by the same distance is a fair, faster O(n) average alternative, though it leaves the k obstacles in no particular order, and sorting those k afterwards to report them nearest first adds back O(k log k).

This is LeetCode's Search a 2D Matrix. The pattern is a single binary search over the grid read as one sorted array, laid out row by row. Index

c.v: It is O(log(r·c)) time and O(1) extra space, one binary search over

candidates rather than one search per row. The edge cases are a grid with no rows, a grid with one empty row, and a target at the first or the last cell, all four covered above. Starting at the top right corner and stepping left when the cell is too large or down when it is too small also finds the target, in O(r + c) time; it is a fair answer, though slower than the bound this statement asks for once the grid stops being close to square.
